micro_skills.subtopic: Arc Lengths and Areas for Parametric Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Surface area of revolution for a parametric curve
definitions: Rotating C: x=f(t), y=g(t), a≤t≤b about the x-axis gives S=2π∫[a,b]|g(t)|√([f'(t)]^2+[g'(t)]^2)dt; about the y-axis, S=2π∫[a,b]|f(t)|√([f'(t)]^2+[g'(t)]^2)dt. The absolute value is essential since the radius of revolution cannot be negative.

theorems.name: Parametric surface area of revolution
theorems.statement: About x-axis: S=2π∫[a,b]|g(t)|√([f'(t)]^2+[g'(t)]^2)dt. About y-axis: S=2π∫[a,b]|f(t)|√([f'(t)]^2+[g'(t)]^2)dt.
conditions: curve does not cross the axis of rotation within the interval (or the absolute value correctly handles sign but the geometric interpretation needs care if it does)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the surface area generated by rotating a parametric curve about the x-axis.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate x=t^2, y=2t, 0≤t≤2, about the x-axis; find the surface area.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A parametric curve is rotated about the x-axis and surface area is requested — apply S=2π∫|g(t)|ds with the radius given by |g(t)| (the y-coordinate), not f(t).
method_plan: Compute f'(t), g'(t) and form ds
Set up S=2π∫|g(t)|ds over the given range
Integrate, using substitution if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ds
M1: correct radius |g(t)| identified (rotation about x-axis)
A1: correct substitution/integration
A1: correct final surface area

common_errors.description: Using f(t) as the radius instead of g(t) when rotating about the x-axis
Omitting the absolute value around g(t) (relevant if g(t) could be negative on the interval)
Errors in the substitution to integrate t√(t^2+1)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the surface area generated by rotating a named curve (e.g. the astroid) about an axis, using symmetry to simplify.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate the astroid x=a cos^3t, y=a sin^3t about the x-axis (upper half, 0≤t≤π, doubled for the full surface); find the surface area.
question_archetypes.answer: ds=3a cos t sin t dt on [0,π/2] (by symmetry compute the upper-right quarter and combine); S=2·2π∫[0,π/2]a sin^3t·3a cos t sin t dt=12πa^2∫[0,π/2]sin^4t cos t dt=12πa^2/5
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is a named symmetric curve (astroid) and the problem requires identifying which portion of the parameter range to integrate over (avoiding double-counting or sign ambiguity) before doubling/multiplying by the appropriate symmetry factor.
method_plan: Identify the curve's symmetry and restrict to a sub-interval where g(t) (or f(t)) doesn't change sign
Set up and simplify the surface area integral over that sub-interval
Apply the correct symmetry multiplier to get the total surface area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct restriction to a sign-consistent sub-interval
M1: correct simplified ds and integrand
A1: correct integration (e.g. via u=sin t substitution)
A1: correct final surface area including the correct symmetry factor

common_errors.description: Integrating over the full range without addressing sign changes in g(t), leading to incorrect cancellation instead of the intended doubling
Errors in the substitution for ∫sin^4t cos t dt
Using the wrong symmetry multiplier for the specific curve/axis combination

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the surface area generated by rotating a parametric curve about the y-axis.
question_archetypes.example: Rotate x=t, y=t^2, 0≤t≤1, about the y-axis; find the surface area.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Rotation is explicitly about the y-axis rather than the x-axis, so the radius in the surface-area formula must be |f(t)| (the x-coordinate), not |g(t)|.
method_plan: Compute f'(t), g'(t) and form ds
Set up S=2π∫|f(t)|ds (radius = x-coordinate, since rotating about the y-axis)
Integrate, using substitution as needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ds
M1: correct radius |f(t)| identified for y-axis rotation
A1: correct substitution/integration
A1: correct final surface area

common_errors.description: Defaulting to g(t) as the radius (correct for x-axis rotation) even though the axis here is the y-axis
Errors in the u-substitution
Dropping the factor of 2π

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.subtopic: Arc Lengths and Areas for Parametric Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Area enclosed by a parametric curve
definitions: The signed area under a parametric curve x=f(t), y=g(t) is A=∫[a,b]g(t)f'(t)dt; for a non-self-intersecting closed curve, A=∫g(t)f'(t)dt if traversed clockwise, A=-∫g(t)f'(t)dt if traversed counterclockwise (equivalently, using x dy with f(t)g'(t)).

theorems.name: Parametric area formula
theorems.statement: A=∫[a,b]g(t)f'(t)dt (signed). For a simple closed curve, counterclockwise traversal gives A=-∫g(t)f'(t)dt (a positive result for a region enclosing the origin's usual orientation); clockwise gives A=+∫g(t)f'(t)dt.
conditions: curve does not self-intersect (for the closed-curve sign convention to give the enclosed area directly)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area enclosed by a parametrized ellipse (or similar simple closed curve), and verify against a known formula.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area enclosed by x=a cos t, y=b sin t, 0≤t≤2π (counterclockwise), and confirm it matches πab.
question_archetypes.answer: A=-∫[0,2π]b sin t·(-a sin t)dt=ab∫[0,2π]sin^2t dt=ab·π=πab ✓
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A standard closed curve (ellipse, circle) is parametrized with an evident direction of traversal, and the enclosed area is requested, ideally checked against the known geometric formula.
method_plan: Determine the direction of traversal (clockwise or counterclockwise) from how t increases
Apply the correctly-signed area formula
Evaluate and compare to the known area formula if available, as a check
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct direction of traversal identified
M1: correctly signed formula applied
A1: correct integral evaluated
A1: correct comparison/verification against the known area

common_errors.description: Using the wrong sign for the direction of traversal, getting a negative area without catching the error
Errors in ∫sin^2t dt (forgetting the power-reduction identity)
Not checking the result against the known area formula when one is available, missing a chance to catch a sign error

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area under one arch of a non-closed parametric curve (like the cycloid) using the direct A=∫g f' dt formula (not the closed-curve sign convention).
question_archetypes.example: Find the area under one arch of the cycloid x=a(t-sin t), y=a(1-cos t), 0≤t≤2π.
question_archetypes.answer: A=∫[0,2π]a(1-cos t)·a(1-cos t)dt=a^2∫[0,2π](1-cos t)^2dt=3πa^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve in question is a single arch of an open (non-closed) curve like the cycloid, sitting above the x-axis — the direct formula A=∫g(t)f'(t)dt applies without needing the closed-curve clockwise/counterclockwise sign convention.
method_plan: Confirm the region is simply 'under the curve' (like the standard y=f(x) area, not an enclosed closed-curve region)
Set up A=∫g(t)f'(t)dt over the given range
Expand and integrate, using trig identities as needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly recognizes this as the direct (non-closed-curve) area formula
M1: correct integral setup
A1: correct expansion of (1-cos t)^2
A1: correct final evaluation

common_errors.description: Applying the closed-curve sign convention (clockwise/counterclockwise) to a curve that is not actually a closed loop
Errors expanding (1-cos t)^2 or integrating cos^2t
Not verifying dx/dt≥0 (needed to ensure the direct area formula's sign convention matches the usual left-to-right area under a curve)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine the direction of traversal of a closed parametric curve algebraically (rather than by inspection), and apply the correct sign in the area formula.
question_archetypes.example: For x=cos(2t), y=sin(2t), 0≤t≤π, determine the direction of traversal and find the enclosed area of the unit circle.
question_archetypes.answer: dx/dt=-2sin2t, dy/dt=2cos2t; at t=0, position (1,0) moving in direction (0,2) i.e. upward — this matches counterclockwise motion; A=-∫[0,π]sin2t·(-2sin2t)dt=2∫[0,π]sin^2(2t)dt=2·(π/2)=π, matching the known area π(1)^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The direction of traversal is not obviously stated or visually given — it must be determined algebraically (e.g. by checking the velocity direction at a sample point) before choosing the correct sign convention for the closed-curve area formula.
method_plan: Evaluate the position and velocity vector at a sample parameter value
Use the velocity direction to determine clockwise vs. counterclockwise traversal
Apply the correctly-signed area formula and verify against the known area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct velocity vector computed at a sample point
M1: correct determination of traversal direction from that vector
A1: correctly signed area formula applied
A1: correct final area matching the known value

common_errors.description: Assuming a default direction (e.g. always counterclockwise) without actually checking via the velocity vector
Errors evaluating the sample point's velocity vector
Not using the known area (π for a unit circle) as a check on the computed sign

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Converting between polar and rectangular coordinates/equations
definitions: A point's polar coordinates [r,θ]: r=distance from the pole, θ=angle from the polar axis. Non-uniqueness: [r,θ]=[r,θ+2nπ]=[-r,θ+π]; the origin is [0,θ] for any θ. Conversion: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ, x^2+y^2=r^2, tanθ=y/x. Converting a polar equation r=f(θ) to Cartesian often uses multiplying both sides by r to introduce x^2+y^2 and r cosθ=x, r sinθ=y.

theorems.name: Polar-rectangular conversion
theorems.statement: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ, x^2+y^2=r^2, tanθ=y/x (for x≠0). [r,θ] and [-r,θ+π] represent the same point; the pole is [0,θ] for every θ.
conditions: conversion of tanθ=y/x requires selecting the correct quadrant, not just the arctan principal value

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Convert a polar equation to Cartesian form and identify the resulting curve.
question_archetypes.example: Convert r=4 sinθ to Cartesian form and identify the curve.
question_archetypes.answer: Multiply by r: r^2=4r sinθ ⇒ x^2+y^2=4y ⇒ x^2+(y-2)^2=4 — circle of radius 2 centered at (0,2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A polar equation r=f(θ) is given directly and Cartesian identification is requested — multiply through by r (or another appropriate factor) to introduce x^2+y^2, x, or y directly.
method_plan: Multiply both sides by r (or another suitable factor) to create x^2+y^2, r cosθ, or r sinθ terms
Substitute the polar-rectangular relations
Complete the square if needed and identify the resulting curve
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct multiplication step introducing convertible terms
M1: correct substitution of x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ, x^2+y^2=r^2
A1: correct completion of the square if needed
A1: correct identification of the curve

common_errors.description: Attempting to substitute x=r cosθ directly without first multiplying by r, getting stuck with an unconvertible r alone
Errors completing the square after substitution
Leaving the answer in a partially converted form without stating the curve's identity/type

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find multiple valid polar representations of the same point, using the non-uniqueness relations.
question_archetypes.example: Give three different polar representations [r,θ] of the rectangular point (0,-2).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks for multiple (not just one) valid polar coordinate representations of a single point, testing understanding that polar coordinates are not unique.
method_plan: Find one straightforward representation [r,θ] with r≥0 and θ in a standard range
Generate additional equivalent representations using [r,θ+2nπ]
Generate a representation using negative r via [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π]
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct primary [r,θ] representation with r≥0
M1: correct additional representation via added 2nπ
A1: correct negative-r representation via the θ+π shift
A1: verifies all three convert back to the same rectangular point

common_errors.description: Believing a point has only one valid polar representation
Errors computing r or θ for the initial representation
Forgetting the negative-r convention [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π] as one of the ways to generate an equivalent representation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Convert a Cartesian equation to polar form, and simplify to identify the curve type from the polar equation alone.
question_archetypes.example: Convert x^2+y^2=2x to polar form.
question_archetypes.answer: r^2=2r cosθ ⇒ r=2cosθ (r≠0 case) — a circle through the origin, center on the polar axis
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem gives a Cartesian equation first and asks for the polar equivalent, requiring the reverse substitution (x^2+y^2=r^2, x=r cosθ) and simplification, potentially dividing out a common factor of r.
method_plan: Substitute x^2+y^2=r^2 and x=r cosθ (or y=r sinθ) into the Cartesian equation
Simplify, dividing out any common nonzero factor of r carefully
Note any special case (like r=0, the origin) separately if division by r was performed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct substitution of polar relations
M1: correct simplification, tracking any division by r
A1: correct final simplified polar equation
A1: notes the r=0 case is not lost/misrepresented by the division

common_errors.description: Errors substituting x=r cosθ correctly into a mixed x,y expression
Dividing by r without acknowledging that r=0 (the origin) is a solution that may or may not still be captured by the simplified equation
Not recognizing the resulting equation's curve type from the standard named-curve list

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Sketching named polar curves using zeros and symmetry
definitions: A polar graph r=f(θ) passes through the origin in direction θ whenever f(θ)=0 — always locate these directions first when sketching. Standard named curves: circle r=a; line θ=β; circle through origin r=2a cosθ (center on polar axis) or r=2a sinθ (center on y-axis); cardioid r=a(1±cosθ) or a(1±sinθ) (cusp at origin); rose r=cos(nθ) or sin(nθ) (n leaves if n odd, 2n leaves if n even); lemniscate r^2=cos(2θ) (figure-eight); spirals r=θ (Archimedean) or r=e^{θ/3} (logarithmic).

theorems.name: Rotating a polar graph
theorems.statement: r=f(θ-θ0) is r=f(θ) rotated by angle θ0 about the origin.

formulas: rose: r=cos(nθ) or sin(nθ), n leaves (n odd) or 2n leaves (n even)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Sketch (or describe key features of) a cardioid, locating its cusp direction, maximum r, and axis of symmetry.
question_archetypes.example: Describe the key features of r=a(1-cosθ) for sketching.
question_archetypes.answer: Enters origin (cusp) at θ=0 (since f(0)=0); maximum r=2a at θ=π; symmetric about the polar axis (θ=0 line)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The equation is recognizably a cardioid (r=a(1±cosθ) or a(1±sinθ) form) and the problem asks for the key sketching features rather than a full point-by-point plot.
method_plan: Find where f(θ)=0 to locate the cusp direction
Find the maximum value of r and the θ where it occurs
Identify the axis of symmetry from the form (cos → polar axis, sin → vertical axis)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct cusp direction from f(θ)=0
M1: correct maximum r and its direction
A1: correct axis of symmetry identified
A1: coherent overall description consistent with all three features

common_errors.description: Not checking f(θ)=0 first, sketching without locating the cusp direction accurately
Confusing which sign/trig function corresponds to which axis of symmetry (cos vs sin, + vs -)
Errors finding the θ that maximizes r

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine the number of leaves (petals) of a rose curve r=cos(nθ) or sin(nθ), and the θ-range needed to trace it exactly once.
question_archetypes.example: How many leaves does r=cos(3θ) have, and over what θ-range is it traced exactly once?
question_archetypes.answer: n=3 is odd, so 3 leaves, traced once over θ∈[0,π)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is explicitly a rose r=cos(nθ) or sin(nθ) and the problem asks about leaf count and/or the parameter range for a single full trace — testing the odd/even n distinction.
method_plan: Determine whether n is odd or even
Apply the corresponding leaf-count rule (n leaves for odd n, 2n for even n)
State the θ-range needed: [0,π) for odd n, [0,2π) for even n
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct determination of odd/even n
M1: correct leaf count from the appropriate rule
A1: correct θ-range for a single complete trace

common_errors.description: Applying the wrong rule (e.g. always assuming n leaves regardless of parity)
Using the wrong θ-range (e.g. [0,π) for an even n, which would only trace half the curve)
Stating leaf count without the corresponding correct θ-range when both were requested

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine the valid domain of θ for a lemniscate (or other curve with r^2=g(θ), requiring g(θ)≥0), and sketch accordingly.
question_archetypes.example: Find the valid θ-values for r^2=cos(2θ), and describe the resulting sketch.
question_archetypes.answer: Need cos(2θ)≥0: -π/4≤θ≤π/4 or 3π/4≤θ≤5π/4 (mod 2π); the curve is a figure-eight (two loops) along the polar axis, with no points where cos(2θ)<0 (r would be imaginary there)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The polar equation is given implicitly in r^2 (not solved explicitly for r), requiring the domain restriction g(θ)≥0 before r=±√g(θ) makes sense — a key step often skipped when sketching lemniscates.
method_plan: Solve the inequality g(θ)≥0 (here cos(2θ)≥0) to find the valid θ-domain
Recognize r=±√g(θ) gives two values of r for each valid θ (or interpret via the standard lemniscate shape)
Sketch only over the valid domain, noting the excluded θ-ranges produce no real points
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly solves the inequality for the valid θ-domain
M1: correctly interprets the ± ambiguity in r=±√g(θ)
A1: correct sketch/description restricted to the valid domain
A1: explicitly notes why the excluded θ-ranges give no real curve points

common_errors.description: Attempting to sketch the curve over all θ∈[0,2π) without first restricting to where cos(2θ)≥0, leading to attempting to take the square root of a negative number
Errors solving the inequality cos(2θ)≥0
Not explaining why parts of the naive full range are excluded

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Polar equation of a conic with focus at the origin
definitions: A conic with focus at the origin, directrix x=-p, eccentricity ε has polar equation r=εp/(1-ε cosθ) — ellipse if ε<1, parabola if ε=1, hyperbola if ε>1 (asymptote directions occur where 1-ε cosθ=0). Analogous forms exist for directrices at x=p, y=-p, y=p (changing the sign and swapping cos/sin).

theorems.name: Polar conic equation
theorems.statement: r=εp/(1-ε cosθ) for a conic with focus at the origin, directrix x=-p, eccentricity ε. Ellipse if ε<1, parabola if ε=1, hyperbola if ε>1.
conditions: p>0 is the distance from focus to directrix
the specific sign/trig function (±cosθ vs ±sinθ) depends on the directrix's location and orientation

formulas: ε<1: ellipse, ε=1: parabola, ε>1: hyperbola

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a polar conic equation, identify the eccentricity and the type of conic.
question_archetypes.example: Classify the conic r=6/(2-3cosθ).
question_archetypes.answer: Rewrite dividing by 2: r=3/(1-1.5cosθ), so ε=1.5>1 — a hyperbola
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A polar equation in (or convertible to) the standard conic form r=εp/(1-ε cosθ) is given, and only the classification (ellipse/parabola/hyperbola) is requested.
method_plan: Rewrite the equation so the denominator's constant term is 1 (divide through if necessary)
Read off ε as the coefficient of cosθ (or sinθ) in the denominator
Classify based on ε<1, =1, or >1
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly rewrites to standard form with denominator constant 1
M1: correct ε identified
A1: correct classification

common_errors.description: Forgetting to divide through so the constant term is exactly 1 before reading off ε
Confusing ε with p, or reading off the wrong coefficient
Not showing the rewriting step, jumping to a possibly incorrect ε

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a polar conic equation, find the eccentricity, the value of p, and the location/equation of the directrix.
question_archetypes.example: For r=4/(1-0.5cosθ), find ε, p, and the directrix.
question_archetypes.answer: ε=0.5, εp=4 ⇒ p=8; directrix x=-p=-8
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The equation is already in (or easily rewritten to) standard form, and the problem asks for the underlying geometric data (p and the directrix equation), not just the conic type.
method_plan: Identify ε directly from the denominator
Use the numerator εp to solve for p
State the directrix's equation based on the identified form (x=-p for this standard form)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct ε
M1: correct p from εp=numerator
A1: correct directrix equation
A1: correct sign consistent with the specific standard form used (± cosθ or sinθ)

common_errors.description: Errors solving εp=(numerator) for p
Using the wrong directrix orientation/sign for the specific trig form given (e.g. assuming x=-p when the equation is actually the y-directrix form)
Giving p without stating the actual directrix equation when both were requested

question_archetypes.prompt_template: For a polar conic equation representing a hyperbola, find the asymptote directions (angles) by finding where the denominator vanishes.
question_archetypes.example: Find the asymptote directions of the hyperbola r=4/(1-2cosθ).
question_archetypes.answer: ε=2; asymptote directions where 1-2cosθ=0, i.e. cosθ=1/2, so θ=±π/3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The polar conic is classified (or recognizable) as a hyperbola (ε>1), and the problem specifically asks for the asymptote directions, which correspond to the θ-values where r→∞ (denominator → 0).
method_plan: Confirm ε>1 (hyperbola case)
Set the denominator 1-ε cosθ (or the appropriate variant) equal to 0 and solve for θ
Interpret these θ-values as the asymptote directions from the origin/focus
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly confirms the hyperbola case (ε>1)
M1: correctly sets up and solves the denominator-zero equation
A1: correct θ-values found
A1: correct interpretation as asymptote directions

common_errors.description: Not recognizing that r→∞ (denominator→0) is exactly the condition defining an asymptote direction
Errors solving cosθ=1/ε for θ
Attempting this for an ellipse or parabola (ε≤1), where the denominator never vanishes and no such asymptote directions exist

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Finding all intersections of two polar curves (including hidden origin intersections)
definitions: Solving f(θ)=g(θ) finds intersections that occur at the same θ for both curves, but this can miss valid intersection points — in particular, both curves may pass through the origin at different θ-values, making the origin a 'hidden' intersection not caught by the direct equation. Coincidences via [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π] must also be checked.

theorems.name: Complete intersection-finding procedure
theorems.statement: To find all intersections of r=f(θ) and r=g(θ): (1) solve f(θ)=g(θ) for same-θ intersections; (2) separately check whether f(θ1)=0 for some θ1 and g(θ2)=0 for some θ2 (possibly θ1≠θ2) — if so, the origin is also a common point; (3) check for coincidences using the equivalent representation [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π].
conditions: applies whenever both curves are polar curves through possibly-differing θ ranges

formulas: hidden origin check: does f(θ1)=0 and g(θ2)=0 for some θ1,θ2 (possibly different)?

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find all intersections of two polar curves, explicitly including a check for a hidden intersection at the origin.
question_archetypes.example: Find all intersections of r=sinθ and r=1-sinθ.
question_archetypes.answer: sinθ=1-sinθ ⇒ sinθ=1/2 ⇒ θ=π/6,5π/6, giving [1/2,π/6] and [1/2,5π/6]; ALSO both pass through the origin (sinθ=0 at θ=0 for the first; 1-sinθ=0 at θ=π/2 for the second) — the origin is a third intersection
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Two polar curves are given and 'find all intersections' is requested — a strong cue to check the origin separately in addition to solving f(θ)=g(θ) directly.
method_plan: Solve f(θ)=g(θ) for same-θ intersections
Separately check whether each curve passes through the origin (f(θ)=0 or g(θ)=0 for some θ, possibly different for each curve)
Report the complete list of intersections, including the origin if applicable
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct same-θ intersections from solving f(θ)=g(θ)
M1: correctly checks each curve individually for passing through the origin
A1: correctly identifies the origin as an additional intersection when applicable
A1: complete, correctly labeled final list of all intersection points

common_errors.description: Only solving f(θ)=g(θ) and stopping there, missing the separately-checked origin intersection
Checking only one curve for passing through the origin instead of both
Not clearly explaining why the origin counts as an intersection despite not solving f(θ)=g(θ) at any single θ

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find an intersection of two polar curves that is only revealed by using the equivalent representation [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π], not by solving f(θ)=g(θ) directly.
question_archetypes.example: Show that r=cosθ and r=-cos θ... [general framing] find all intersections of r=2cosθ and r=2sinθ, including any found only via the negative-r equivalence, if applicable.
question_archetypes.answer: Direct: 2cosθ=2sinθ ⇒ tanθ=1 ⇒ θ=π/4,5π/4, giving points [√2,π/4] and [-√2,5π/4] (same point as [√2,π/4] via the sign-flip, so really one point at θ=π/4) plus the origin (each curve passes through it at a different θ: cosθ=0 at θ=π/2, sinθ=0 at θ=0)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem explicitly asks to consider the negative-r equivalence [r,θ]=[-r,θ+π] as a potential source of additional intersections not caught by directly solving f(θ)=g(θ), typically flagged when curves involve odd symmetry or sign ambiguity.
method_plan: Solve f(θ)=g(θ) directly for the 'obvious' intersections
Check whether re-writing one curve's equation using the [-r,θ+π] equivalence produces additional matching solutions not found directly
Check the origin separately as in the standard procedure, and consolidate the final list without double-counting coincident points
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct direct intersections from f(θ)=g(θ)
M1: correctly explores the negative-r equivalence for additional coincidences
A1: correctly checks the origin separately
A1: correctly consolidates the final list, avoiding double-counting of points reached via different θ but representing the same location

common_errors.description: Never considering the [-r,θ+π] equivalence as a possible source of additional (or coincident) intersections
Double-counting the same geometric point when it's reached via two different valid θ representations
Errors solving tanθ=1 or checking the resulting r values via the sign-flip relation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a claimed count of intersection points for two polar curves, verify it is correct (or correct it) by systematically applying the full intersection-finding procedure.
question_archetypes.example: A student claims r=1+cosθ and r=3cosθ intersect at exactly 2 points. Verify or correct this claim.
question_archetypes.answer: Direct: 1+cosθ=3cosθ ⇒ cosθ=1/2 ⇒ θ=±π/3, giving [3/2,±π/3] (2 points); origin check: 1+cosθ=0 at θ=π, and 3cosθ=0 at θ=π/2 — both curves DO pass through the origin (at different θ), so the origin is a THIRD intersection point; the student's claim of exactly 2 is incorrect — there are 3
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A specific numeric claim about the number of intersections is presented for verification, and the systematic full procedure (direct equation solving, origin check, sign-flip check) must be applied methodically to confirm or refute it.
method_plan: Apply the direct f(θ)=g(θ) solving step and count those solutions
Apply the origin check step, adding it to the count if both curves pass through the origin
Apply the sign-flip check if relevant, then compare the total count to the claim and correct if needed
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct direct-solution count
M1: correct origin check performed and correctly incorporated
A1: correct sign-flip check (if relevant to this pair of curves)
A1: correct final count with clear identification of any error in the original claim

common_errors.description: Accepting a stated count without independently re-deriving it via the full systematic procedure
Forgetting to check the origin, which is precisely the step most often responsible for undercounting
Not explicitly stating which specific intersection point was missing from the original (incorrect) claim

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.subtopic: Slopes, Areas, and Arc Lengths for Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Tangent-radius angle ψ and tangent slope for a polar curve
definitions: At P=[r,θ] (not the origin) on r=f(θ), if ψ is the angle between the radius OP and the tangent line, tanψ=f(θ)/f'(θ)=r/(dr/dθ); ψ=π/2 (tangent ⟂ radius) when f'(θ)=0. If f(θ0)=0, the tangent line at the origin is simply θ=θ0. To find the actual Cartesian slope dy/dx, convert to x=f(θ)cosθ, y=f(θ)sinθ and use the parametric-curve slope formula.

theorems.name: Tangent-radius angle
theorems.statement: tanψ=r/(dr/dθ)=f(θ)/f'(θ) for the angle ψ between the radius OP and the tangent line at P=[r,θ] (r≠0).
conditions: P is not the origin (r≠0)
for the origin itself, the tangent is simply the line θ=θ0 where f(θ0)=0

formulas: at the origin (f(θ0)=0): tangent line is θ=θ0
Cartesian slope: convert to x=f(θ)cosθ, y=f(θ)sinθ, use dy/dx=(dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the angle ψ between the radius and tangent line at a specified point on a polar curve.
question_archetypes.example: Find ψ for r=θ at θ=π/2.
question_archetypes.answer: f(θ)=θ, f'(θ)=1; tanψ=θ/1=θ; at θ=π/2: tanψ=π/2, so ψ=tan^{-1}(π/2)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks specifically for the angle ψ between the tangent and the radius (not the Cartesian slope dy/dx) — apply tanψ=r/(dr/dθ) directly.
method_plan: Compute f(θ) and f'(θ)
Form tanψ=f(θ)/f'(θ)
Evaluate at the given θ and solve for ψ if a numeric angle is requested
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f(θ), f'(θ)
M1: correct formula tanψ=f/f' applied
A1: correct evaluation at the given θ
A1: correct final ψ (or tanψ) as requested

common_errors.description: Confusing ψ (angle to the radius) with the Cartesian slope angle (angle to the x-axis) — these are generally different quantities
Errors evaluating f(θ)/f'(θ) at the specific θ
Giving tanψ when ψ itself was explicitly requested, or vice versa

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the actual Cartesian slope dy/dx of the tangent line to a polar curve at a given point, by converting to parametric x(θ), y(θ) form.
question_archetypes.example: Find the slope of the tangent line to r=θ at θ=π/2.
question_archetypes.answer: x=θcosθ, y=θsinθ; dx/dθ=cosθ-θsinθ, dy/dθ=sinθ+θcosθ; at θ=π/2: dx/dθ=-π/2, dy/dθ=1; slope=dy/dx=1/(-π/2)=-2/π
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for the actual slope of the tangent line (dy/dx, as one would graph it in the xy-plane), not the angle ψ relative to the radius — requires converting to x(θ), y(θ) first.
method_plan: Write x=f(θ)cosθ, y=f(θ)sinθ
Differentiate both with respect to θ using the product rule
Evaluate dy/dx=(dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ) at the given θ
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct x(θ), y(θ) parametrization
M1: correct derivatives via the product rule
A1: correct evaluation at the given θ
A1: correct final Cartesian slope

common_errors.description: Using tanψ=r/(dr/dθ) directly as if it were dy/dx (it is not — ψ is measured from the radius, not the x-axis)
Forgetting the product rule when differentiating f(θ)cosθ or f(θ)sinθ
Sign errors evaluating the derivatives at the specific θ

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the tangent line direction(s) at the origin for a polar curve, using the directions where f(θ)=0.
question_archetypes.example: Find the tangent line(s) at the origin for the cardioid r=1+cosθ.
question_archetypes.answer: f(θ)=0 at θ=π (only solution in [0,2π)); tangent line at the origin is θ=π (the negative x-axis direction)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The point of interest is explicitly the origin (pole), where the general tanψ=r/(dr/dθ) formula doesn't directly apply (since r=0 there) — the tangent direction is instead simply θ=θ0 for any θ0 with f(θ0)=0.
method_plan: Solve f(θ)=0 to find all directions θ0 at which the curve passes through the origin
State that each such θ0 gives a tangent line direction θ=θ0 at the origin
If multiple θ0 solutions exist, list all resulting tangent directions (the curve may pass through the origin more than once)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly solves f(θ)=0 for all θ0 in the relevant range
M1: correctly identifies the tangent line at the origin as θ=θ0 for each solution
A1: correct final tangent direction(s)
A1: notes if multiple distinct tangent directions exist at the origin (curve crosses itself there)

common_errors.description: Attempting to apply tanψ=r/(dr/dθ) at the origin, where r=0 makes the formula meaningless/undefined in the usual sense
Finding only one solution to f(θ)=0 when multiple exist within the relevant range, missing additional tangent directions
Not stating the tangent line as the simple polar equation θ=θ0

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.subtopic: Slopes, Areas, and Arc Lengths for Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Horizontal and vertical tangents of a polar curve
definitions: To find horizontal/vertical tangent points on r=f(θ), convert to x=f(θ)cosθ, y=f(θ)sinθ and find where dy/dθ=0 (horizontal, with dx/dθ≠0) or dx/dθ=0 (vertical, with dy/dθ≠0) — dr/dθ=0 alone does NOT by itself indicate a horizontal tangent, a common trap.

theorems.name: Polar horizontal/vertical tangent conditions
theorems.statement: With x=f(θ)cosθ, y=f(θ)sinθ: horizontal tangent where dy/dθ=0, dx/dθ≠0; vertical tangent where dx/dθ=0, dy/dθ≠0.
conditions: must differentiate the CONVERTED x(θ), y(θ), not use dr/dθ=0 directly as a proxy for horizontal tangent

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find all horizontal and vertical tangent points of a cardioid.
question_archetypes.example: Find the horizontal and vertical tangents of r=1+cosθ.
question_archetypes.answer: y=(1+cosθ)sinθ: dy/dθ=(2cosθ-1)(cosθ+1)=0 ⇒ cosθ=1/2 or -1; horizontal at θ=±π/3 (giving [3/2,±π/3]), θ=π gives r=0 (cusp, no ordinary tangent). x=(1+cosθ)cosθ: dx/dθ=-sinθ(1+2cosθ)=0 ⇒ sinθ=0 or cosθ=-1/2; vertical at θ=0 ([2,0]) and θ=±2π/3 ([1/2,±2π/3])
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A specific named polar curve (cardioid or similar) is given and all horizontal/vertical tangent points are requested — convert to x(θ),y(θ), differentiate, factor, and solve.
method_plan: Write y=f(θ)sinθ and differentiate; factor and solve dy/dθ=0
Write x=f(θ)cosθ and differentiate; factor and solve dx/dθ=0
Exclude any θ where the curve has a cusp (f(θ)=0 at the same θ), and report the remaining points in [r,θ] or (x,y) form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct dy/dθ, correctly factored and solved
M1: correct dx/dθ, correctly factored and solved
A1: correctly excludes the cusp point(s) from the tangent list
A1: correct final list of horizontal and vertical tangent points

common_errors.description: Using dr/dθ=0 directly as the horizontal-tangent condition instead of converting to y=f(θ)sinθ first
Forgetting to check that the OTHER derivative is nonzero at each candidate, or forgetting to exclude the cusp point
Errors factoring the resulting trigonometric polynomial in cosθ

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explicitly identify why dr/dθ=0 alone does not indicate a horizontal tangent, using a specific curve as a counterexample.
question_archetypes.example: For r=1+cosθ, show that dr/dθ=0 at θ=0 does NOT correspond to a horizontal tangent there.
question_archetypes.answer: dr/dθ=-sinθ=0 at θ=0, but computing dy/dθ at θ=0 (from y=(1+cosθ)sinθ): dy/dθ=(2cos0-1)(cos0+1)=(1)(2)=2≠0 — so the tangent at θ=0 is actually vertical (matches dx/dθ=0 there), not horizontal, despite dr/dθ=0
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem is explicitly framed as a 'trap' or misconception check — testing whether the student mistakenly equates dr/dθ=0 with a horizontal tangent, a very common but incorrect shortcut in polar curves.
method_plan: Compute dr/dθ and note where it vanishes
Separately compute dy/dθ (and dx/dθ) at that same θ using the converted x(θ), y(θ) forms
Show explicitly that dr/dθ=0 does not force dy/dθ=0, resolving the apparent paradox
full_mark_rubric: M1: correctly computes dr/dθ and finds where it's zero
M1: correctly computes dy/dθ (and/or dx/dθ) at that θ from the converted forms
A1: correctly shows dy/dθ≠0 there, refuting the horizontal-tangent assumption
A1: clear explanation of why dr/dθ=0 is not equivalent to a horizontal tangent condition

common_errors.description: This IS the target misconception: equating dr/dθ=0 with dy/dθ=0 (horizontal tangent) — the entire point of the archetype is to catch and correct this
Errors differentiating y=f(θ)sinθ via the product rule
Not explicitly contrasting the (wrong) dr/dθ=0 conclusion with the (correct) dy/dθ, dx/dθ analysis

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the horizontal and vertical tangent points of a simple polar circle (not through the origin, or through it), as a warm-up case with a clean answer.
question_archetypes.example: Find the horizontal and vertical tangent points of r=2a cosθ (a circle of radius a centered at (a,0)).
question_archetypes.answer: x=2a cos^2θ, y=2a cosθ sinθ=a sin2θ; dy/dθ=2a cos2θ=0 ⇒ θ=π/4,3π/4 (horizontal tangents); dx/dθ=-2a sin2θ=0 ⇒ θ=0,π/2 (vertical tangents, with θ=π/2 giving the origin, a degenerate case to examine separately)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is a simple, well-understood shape (a circle) given in polar form, useful for confirming the horizontal/vertical tangent method works correctly on a case whose Cartesian tangent points are already geometrically obvious (top/bottom/left/right of the circle).
method_plan: Convert to x(θ), y(θ) and simplify using double-angle identities if helpful
Differentiate and solve for horizontal and vertical tangent θ-values
Cross-check the results against the geometrically obvious top/bottom/left/right points of the circle
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct x(θ), y(θ), simplified via double-angle identities
M1: correct dy/dθ, dx/dθ and correctly solved
A1: correct tangent points identified
A1: cross-check against the known geometric circle confirms the results

common_errors.description: Errors applying double-angle identities to simplify x(θ), y(θ)
Not recognizing θ=π/2 corresponds to the origin (a degenerate point) requiring separate treatment
Not using the circle's known geometry as a sanity check on the computed tangent points

micro_skills.topic: Conics, Parametric Curves, and Polar Curves
micro_skills.subtopic: Slopes, Areas, and Arc Lengths for Polar Curves
micro_skills.micro_skill: Area in polar coordinates
definitions: The area bounded by r=f(θ) and rays θ=α, θ=β is A=½∫[α,β][f(θ)]^2dθ. The area between two polar curves r=f(θ) (outer) and r=g(θ) (inner) over the same angular range is A=½∫[α,β]([f(θ)]^2-[g(θ)]^2)dθ — which curve is outer can switch across sub-ranges, requiring the integral to be split, exactly as with Cartesian area-between-curves problems.

theorems.name: Polar area formula
theorems.statement: A=½∫[α,β][f(θ)]^2dθ for the region bounded by r=f(θ) and θ=α,β. For the area between two curves, A=½∫[α,β]([outer]^2-[inner]^2)dθ.
conditions: α<β, and the region is swept out exactly once as θ ranges over [α,β] (no double-counting/retracing)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area enclosed by a single polar curve over a given angular range (or its full enclosed area using symmetry).
question_archetypes.example: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid r=a(1+cosθ).
question_archetypes.answer: By symmetry, twice the upper half: A=2·½∫[0,π]a^2(1+cosθ)^2dθ=a^2∫[0,π](1+2cosθ+(1+cos2θ)/2)dθ=3πa^2/2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A single named polar curve's total enclosed area is requested — apply the basic polar area formula, using symmetry to reduce to half the range where convenient.
method_plan: Identify the correct angular range that traces the curve exactly once (using symmetry to halve the work if applicable)
Set up A=½∫[f(θ)]^2dθ, expanding the square and using power-reduction identities as needed
Integrate and simplify
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct angular range identified (with symmetry factor if used)
M1: correct expansion of [f(θ)]^2 using power-reduction identities
A1: correct integration
A1: correct final area

common_errors.description: Forgetting the factor of ½ in the polar area formula
Errors expanding (1+cosθ)^2 or applying the power-reduction identity for cos^2θ
Not exploiting symmetry, integrating over the full range unnecessarily (not wrong, but more error-prone)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area inside one polar curve and outside another, over a range where the outer/inner roles don't switch.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area inside the circle r=3sinθ and outside the cardioid r=1+sinθ.
question_archetypes.answer: Intersect where 3sinθ=1+sinθ ⇒ sinθ=1/2 ⇒ θ=π/6,5π/6; on this range the circle is outer (check at θ=π/2: circle gives 3, cardioid gives 2); A=½∫[π/6,5π/6][(3sinθ)^2-(1+sinθ)^2]dθ=π
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The area between two curves is requested, and after finding the intersection angles, a spot-check confirms the same curve is outer throughout the relevant range — no splitting needed.
method_plan: Find the intersection angles by solving f(θ)=g(θ)
Spot-check which curve is outer at a sample angle within the range
Set up A=½∫([outer]^2-[inner]^2)dθ over the intersection range and evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection angles
M1: correct outer/inner identification via a spot check
A1: correct integral setup and expansion
A1: correct final evaluation

common_errors.description: Assuming which curve is outer without actually checking at a sample point, risking a sign error
Errors expanding (3sinθ)^2-(1+sinθ)^2
Forgetting the ½ factor in the polar area-between-curves formula

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the area between two polar curves over a range where the outer and inner curves swap partway through, requiring the integral to be split.
question_archetypes.example: Find the area common to (inside both) r=√2 sinθ and r^2=sin2θ.
question_archetypes.answer: They intersect (besides the origin) where sinθ=cosθ, i.e. θ=π/4; A=½∫[0,π/4]2sin^2θ dθ+½∫[π/4,π/2]sin2θ dθ=π/8 (the 'common area' requires using whichever curve is the boundary — i.e. smaller r — on each sub-range)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks for area common to both curves (inside both), or otherwise implies the identity of the bounding curve changes across the angular range — a signal that the integral must be split at the point where the curves' roles switch.
method_plan: Find where the two curves intersect (other than possibly the origin)
Determine which curve is the relevant boundary (e.g. the smaller r, for 'common to both') on each side of the intersection
Split the integral at the intersection angle and sum the two pieces
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct intersection angle(s) found
M1: correctly identifies which curve bounds the region on each sub-range
A1: correct split integral setup
A1: correct evaluation and sum of both pieces

common_errors.description: Using a single curve's formula across the entire range without checking whether the relevant boundary actually switches partway through
Forgetting to split the integral at the identified switch point
Errors evaluating ∫sin^2θ dθ or ∫sin2θ dθ over the respective sub-ranges

micro_skills.micro_skill: Arc length of a polar curve
definitions: The arc length element for r=f(θ) is ds=√((dr/dθ)^2+r^2)dθ, giving s=∫[α,β]√([f'(θ)]^2+[f(θ)]^2)dθ. As with parametric arc length, simplifying the radicand (often via a half-angle identity) is usually the key step.

theorems.name: Polar arc length
conditions: f' continuous on [α,β]
curve traced exactly once over [α,β] for s to represent the actual arc length without double-counting

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the arc length of a simple polar circle and check it matches the known circumference formula.
question_archetypes.example: Find the total arc length of r=2a cosθ using the polar arc-length formula, and check it matches 2πa.
question_archetypes.answer: f'=-2a sinθ; ds=√(4a^2sin^2θ+4a^2cos^2θ)dθ=2a dθ; traced fully as θ:0→π (period π for this circle, passing through the origin at θ=±π/2): s=∫[0,π]2a dθ=2πa ✓
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is a simple named shape (circle) whose known arc length (circumference) provides an immediate check on the polar arc-length computation — useful for verifying correct setup, especially the correct θ-range for one full trace.
method_plan: Compute f'(θ) and form the radicand (df/dθ)^2+f(θ)^2, simplifying using Pythagorean identities
Determine the correct θ-range that traces the curve exactly once (may be less than 2π for curves passing through the origin)
Integrate and compare to the known geometric arc length
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radicand simplified via a trig identity
M1: correct θ-range identified for exactly one full trace
A1: correct integration
A1: correct final comparison confirming the known circumference

common_errors.description: Using θ-range [0,2π] when the curve actually closes up (traces fully) over a shorter range like [0,π], causing double-counting
Errors simplifying the radicand via sin^2+cos^2=1
Not using the known circumference as a check on the final answer

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the total arc length of a cardioid using a half-angle identity to simplify the radicand.
question_archetypes.example: Find the total arc length of the cardioid r=a(1+cosθ).
question_archetypes.answer: f'=-a sinθ; ds=√(a^2sin^2θ+a^2(1+cosθ)^2)dθ=a√(2+2cosθ)dθ=a√(4cos^2(θ/2))dθ=2a|cos(θ/2)|dθ; s=2∫[0,π]2a cos(θ/2)dθ=8a (doubling for symmetry, integrating over [0,π] where cos(θ/2)≥0)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is a named curve (cardioid) whose arc-length radicand simplifies dramatically via the identity 1+cosθ=2cos^2(θ/2) — recognizing this is the crucial simplification step, as with several parametric arc-length problems.
method_plan: Compute f'(θ) and form the radicand
Apply the half-angle identity 1+cosθ=2cos^2(θ/2) to simplify to a perfect square under the root
Integrate over the correct range (using symmetry and the correct sign of the resulting cos(θ/2) term)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct radicand formed before simplification
M1: correct application of the half-angle identity
A1: correct integration over the appropriate range, with correct sign handling
A1: correct final arc length, matching the known result 8a

common_errors.description: Not recognizing the half-angle identity, attempting to integrate an unsimplified square root
Errors applying 1+cosθ=2cos^2(θ/2)
Mishandling the absolute value of cos(θ/2) or the symmetry factor over the full range

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the arc length of only a portion (not the full closed curve) of a polar curve between two specified angles.
question_archetypes.example: Find the arc length of the spiral r=e^{θ/3} from θ=0 to θ=2π.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The curve is a spiral (or another curve without an obvious closed/repeating structure), and the arc length is requested only between two specific angles rather than over a 'natural' full-trace range — a more open-ended, less formulaic setup than the closed-curve cases.
method_plan: Compute f'(θ) and form the radicand, simplifying algebraically (factoring out common exponential or power terms)
Set up the arc length integral over exactly the given θ-range (no symmetry shortcut available for a non-repeating spiral)
Integrate and evaluate
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f'(θ)
M1: correct simplified radicand (factoring correctly)
A1: correct integral setup over the specified range
A1: correct final evaluation

common_errors.description: Errors factoring the exponential terms out of the square root
Attempting to apply a symmetry shortcut that doesn't exist for this open (non-closed, non-periodic) spiral
Using the wrong range of integration (e.g. assuming a 'natural' period rather than the explicitly given angles)
